claims.text: The starting material is a titanium–nickel-based high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state produced by powder metallurgy without intentional dispersoids.
The intervention adds approximately 0.5–1 at.% Y2O3 nanoparticles during processing.
Y2O3 nanoparticles will remain as stable nanoscale oxide dispersoids in the relevant elevated-temperature regime.
The oxide dispersoids will be situated both along grain boundaries and within grains.
Y2O3 particles will pin grain boundaries and inhibit grain-boundary migration.
Y2O3 particles will impede dislocation motion through Orowan strengthening.
Inhibiting grain-boundary migration will limit grain coarsening during prolonged elevated-temperature exposure.
Preservation of a refined microstructure will improve retention of microhardness and yield strength after high-temperature exposure.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will have a slower grain-growth rate than the otherwise identical alloy without Y2O3.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will show smaller decreases in hardness and yield strength at elevated temperature than the baseline alloy.
An analogous powder-metallurgy high-entropy alloy exhibits grain growth during prolonged annealing at 1000 °C in argon.
An analogous powder-metallurgy high-entropy alloy softens during prolonged annealing, with hardness decreasing from 1065 HV to 1000 HV after heating for up to 1000 hours.
Long-term annealing at 800–1000 °C in an inert atmosphere is an applicable test regime for evaluating the proposed titanium–nickel alloy intervention.

The intervention will remain effective only if the nanoparticle content is low enough to avoid brittle-phase formation, the particles are distributed uniformly, and the temperature remains below the oxide's stability limit.
The magnitude of mechanical-property improvement may depend on particle-distribution uniformity, Y2O3–matrix interfacial bonding, and stability during cyclic thermal exposure.
